name: Sanjukta Panigrahi
title: Sanjukta Panigrahi: The Work Behind the Dance
description: A dancer’s own recollections, a musical partnership and the performances that other artists came to study.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: At Kalakshetra in Madras, the young Sanjukta Panigrahi did not initially speak Tamil. In an account edited by Julia Varley from her 1996 interview and speech, she remembered using hand gestures to communicate with other children. She stayed for six years. The memory brings an internationally known dancer back to the effort of being a student: learning a language, living away from home and becoming accustomed to a demanding school.

Her mother’s support runs through the same recollection. Sanjukta describes a woman determined that her daughter should learn to dance, even when relatives feared what it would mean for her future. Later, after training in Bharatanatyam, Sanjukta chose to concentrate on Odissi with Kelucharan Mohapatra. These are her remembered choices and relationships, rather than a story of a tradition waiting for one person to discover it.

The Sangeet Natak Akademi’s 1976 award honoured Sanjukta and Raghunath Panigrahi jointly. Its citation is precise about their contributions: she is recognised for Odissi dance, teaching and choreography; he for Odissi music. It records his training as a singer, his early professional work with All India Radio in Cuttack and his rendering of Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda. A joint honour did not make their work interchangeable.

Sanjukta’s own account makes the partnership less effortless than an award citation can suggest. She remembered disagreements about continuing her career, their eventual return to Bhubaneswar in 1966, and Raghunath singing with her increasingly as her performances grew. She also acknowledged the compromises he made in his own career.

That candour matters. It lets us understand a performing partnership as work negotiated between two artists, with separate ambitions and responsibilities. It also keeps the music audible in a story that might otherwise be told through the dancer’s image alone.

Her work also entered an international conversation about performance. ISTA, the International School of Theatre Anthropology, identifies her dance as the opening of its first session in Bonn in October 1980. Its later educational film, made by Eugenio Barba, Claudio Coloberti and Julia Varley, returns to that performance in considering how actors and dancers build presence. This gives a specific meaning to an international contribution: her practice became something fellow performers studied.

Sanjukta can be remembered through each of these relationships: to her teachers, to her mother, to Raghunath and to artists learning across different traditions. Together they give depth to the familiar portrait in dance costume. Behind the celebrated performance stands a person who kept choosing the work, and who was willing to speak about what that choice demanded.
